title: India Signs ₹1,976 Crore Deal With Israel's IAI to Upgrade Navy's Barak Missiles
excerpt: The contract upgrades seven Barak-1 point defence systems — launchers, radars and command systems bought in 2000 — with new hardware and software, with BEL and BDL as IAI's industry partners in India.
body:
• India's Ministry of Defence signed a ₹1,976.40 crore contract with Israel Aerospace Industries on November 18 to upgrade the Barak Point Defence Missile System on Indian Navy warships.
  • The deal covers seven complete Barak-1 systems — vertical launch units, fire-control radars and command systems — first bought in October 2000 for about ₹1,160 crore.
  • Bharat Electronics Ltd and Bharat Dynamics Ltd will act as Israel Aerospace Industries' primary industry partners for the upgrade in India.
  • The Barak-1 is the Navy's close-in air-defence layer against aircraft, anti-ship missiles and drones; an indigenous replacement, the VL-SRSAM, is still in development.

India's Ministry of Defence signed a contract worth ₹1,976.40 crore with Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) on Wednesday, November 18, to upgrade the Barak Point Defence Missile System carried on Indian Navy warships and to manage the ageing system's obsolescence. The contract, signed in New Delhi in the presence of Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, was concluded under the Other Capital Procurement Procedure, the ministry said in a statement.

The work covers a comprehensive upgrade of the system's hardware and software. The ministry said the upgrade would give naval platforms "enhanced features and potent range anti-air defence capability," extending the service relevance of a weapon the Navy has operated for more than two decades.

Seven systems, bought in 2000, get a second life

Through the deal, the ministry intends to upgrade seven complete shipborne Barak-1 anti-missile defence systems, broadly comprising vertical launch units, fire-control radars and command systems, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. India originally bought the systems in October 2000, along with accompanying missiles, in an emergency procurement valued at approximately ₹1,160 crore at the time. Two contracts were signed on October 23, 2000 — a $199.50 million deal with IAI for the seven systems and a $69.13 million contract with Rafael Advanced Defense Systems for 200 missiles, BharatShakti reported.

The Barak systems are installed on an aircraft carrier and on frontline destroyers and frigates. On the Delhi-class destroyers, mid-life refits added eight-cell vertical launch modules, taking their missile-carrying capacity to 32. Defence public sector units Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL) and Bharat Dynamics Ltd (BDL) will act as primary industry partners for IAI in the upgrades, BusinessLine reported.

The close-in layer of a layered shield

Point defence is the last layer of a warship's air defence: the Barak-1 is designed to protect the ship itself against incoming aircraft, anti-ship missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles that have got past longer-range weapons. It sits below the longer-range Barak-8, jointly developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and IAI and inducted into the Navy as the Long Range Surface-to-Air Missile, in the fleet's layered air-defence architecture.

The contract follows an administrative approval granted by the Defence Acquisition Council, chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, at its meeting on August 5, 2025. The ministry has not said which ships will be upgraded first or how long the programme will take.

A deal with a contested past

The original 2000 purchase later courted controversy: the Central Bureau of Investigation probed alleged middleman commissions following the 2001 Tehelka sting operation, before closing the case in December 2013, citing lack of evidence to prosecute suspects. The ministry subsequently approved a follow-on order of 262 additional Barak-1 missiles worth ₹880 crore, BusinessLine reported.

What happens next

The upgraded Barak-1 is expected to remain the Navy's point-defence system until its eventual replacement, the indigenously developed Vertical Launch Short Range Surface-to-Air Missile (VL-SRSAM) being developed by DRDO, is ready for induction. Until then, the ₹1,976.40 crore upgrade is the bridge: it keeps seven systems bought a quarter-century ago operationally relevant against faster and more varied aerial threats.
